<document>
# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
I've read it. Here's my restatement, then my assessment.

## What the report says

**Varden case-processing, 24 months** (7 vs 7 offices, still on their assigned schedules):

| Measure | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% | −3.4% (CI −8.0 to +1.2) |
| Fall in actual hours, timesheets | 13% | 12% |
| Fall in actual hours, system logs (new) | — | 11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% | +9.8% |
| Output per hour, logs | — | +8.5% (CI 3.4 to 13.8) |

Quality, sick days (−27%) and lower resignations all held.

**Mediation.** This was registered at month 11, before the 24-month outcomes existed.
- Meeting time fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week in treated offices, against 7.2 to 7.0 in control.
- Meetings account for 47% of the gain (CI 28 to 66), fatigue for 18% (CI 2 to 34), and 35% is unexplained.

**Unplanned observation.** Two control offices ran a "meeting audit" at month 15 without changing hours. Their meeting time fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours, and their output per hour rose 4.1% against their own prior six months.

**Counter arm.** The county ended it at month 12 because of waiting times (7.3 vs 4.0 minutes). Restoring service would have needed about 12% more staff, at about +9% cost per contact.

**Halden subset** (14 of the 23 organisations with records):
- Three reverted: hospitality, retail and a marketing agency, with output indices of 88–91 at reversion.
- The 11 that continued show record-based output of 96.8 and actual hours down 13.4%, a +11.8% per-hour gain. They have no comparison group and have been selected twice.

**Rebuttals.**
- *Varga and Holm:* the gain survives the standards they themselves recommended.
- *The meta-analysis:* its four long-follow-up studies were all uncontrolled and used scheduled hours, so they cannot show an absence of decay.

The arithmetic checks out: 0.966 / 0.88 ≈ +9.8% and 0.966 / 0.89 ≈ +8.5%.

## Overall verdict

This is the strongest document of the five, and it settles several of the questions I had marked open:
- A per-actual-hour gain persists to 24 months under randomisation, record-based output and two hours measures. Its interval excludes zero by a clear margin.
- The meetings pathway survives a registered test.
- The meta-analysis's "no decay" conclusion rested on exactly the design features the meta-analysis itself showed inflate effects. My concern about that comparison turns out to have been well founded.

The issues below mostly concern how strongly the summary states things, plus one problem the report doesn't notice.

## Problems

**1. Control offices adopted part of the treatment, and the report doesn't consider what that does to the 24-month estimate.** Two of the seven control offices cut meetings at month 15 and gained about 4% in output per hour. That partly delivers the treatment to the control group, which is exactly what office-level randomisation was meant to prevent. The audits may also have been prompted by staff knowing the trial was under way.

The effect on the estimate is roughly this: averaged across the control arm, a 4.1% gain in two of seven offices is about 1.2 points over the final nine months. That lowers the treated-versus-control gap, and it could account for a meaningful part of the 2.7-point fall from 12.5% to 9.8%.

The report treats the audit only as evidence that reorganisation alone might work. It should also report the 24-month estimate with those two offices excluded, or with their post-audit months excluded, as a labelled sensitivity analysis. The "decline" may be partly an artefact of the control arm improving.

**2. The summary overstates the decline by mixing measures, and the decline itself is uncertain.**
- **Mixed measures.** The summary's "12.5% to 8.5%" compares a timesheet figure at nine months with a log figure at 24 months. The like-for-like comparison is 12.5% to 9.8%, which the body correctly uses.
- **Overlapping intervals.** The two timesheet intervals overlap almost entirely (6.9 to 18.4 vs 4.6 to 15.2). The body's wording, "consistent with some fading", is right. "Declined by about a quarter" in §5 treats a point-estimate change as an established decline.
- **What's actually established.** The gain persists. Some fading is plausible but not demonstrated, and contamination (point 1) may account for part of the apparent fall.

**3. "Confirms" is stronger than a mediation analysis can deliver.** The test is registered and the result is substantial, so the meetings pathway now deserves real weight. But:
- **Meeting cuts weren't randomised.** Offices whose managers cut more meetings may differ in other ways, such as management quality. The 47% depends on there being no confounding between mediator and outcome, which the Limitations section concedes.
- **Cluster count.** "A larger sample of office-months" doesn't increase the number of independent units, which is still 14 offices. If the intervals treat office-months as independent, they are too narrow. The report should state how they were computed; a cluster bootstrap or randomisation inference would be appropriate.

The accurate summary is that a registered test supports meetings as a substantial pathway, probably larger than fatigue, under the usual mediation assumptions.

Separately, the new pre-period meeting data (7.4 vs 7.2) close the caveat I raised at nine months: baseline meeting time was balanced. The rough calculation I made then also now holds up better. A large share of the hours cut came out of meeting time.

**4. It isn't clear what the system logs measure, or what their baseline is.**
- **Baseline.** Log data are described as "added" at follow-up, yet the 11% figure is a difference-in-differences estimate, which needs pre-period log data. Were these retrieved from historical system records? The report should say.
- **Scope.** If "active log-in time" captures only time working on cases, it excludes meetings. It would then measure case-working time, not total working time, and "logs show slightly more work than timesheets" would be comparing different things. It would also change how output per log-measured hour, and hence the mediation, should be read.

This doesn't undermine the result, but the definition determines what the 8.5% means.

**5. The Halden follow-up needs more careful framing.**
- **"Upper bound" is the wrong term.** Without a comparison group, secular trends could push the figure either way. "Optimistic estimate for self-selected continuers" is accurate.
- **The 11.8% at 24 months can't be compared with Varga and Holm's 10.8% at six months.** They come from different subsets (11 vs 17 organisations), so the pair says nothing about decay.
- **Selection compounds.** 14 of 23 responded, and the 23 were themselves the subset that submitted records.
- **The marketing agency doesn't fit "coverage obligations".** Client deadlines describe deadline-driven discretionary work. That is a useful counterexample to the clean binary, and it supports the meta-analysis's own limitation about classification, but the summary groups it with the coverage cases.

**6. A minor point on authorship.** The trial's own authors, with a Halden co-author, are here assessing critiques of their work. That doesn't weaken the findings, and the registered protocol filed at month 11 is what earns the results their weight. It does make the sensitivity analyses above more valuable, since it is the authors' own critics who most need to see them.

## Where the questions now stand

| Question | Status |
|---|---|
| Headline 20%+ figures are inflated | **Settled.** |
| A real per-actual-hour gain exists | **Settled**, now to 24 months in a randomised setting. "Entirely an artifact" is refuted. |
| Size in discretionary work | **About 8–12%.** Varden 8.5–9.8% at 24 months, controlled discretionary studies 9.6%. |
| Gain persists beyond a year | **Settled to 24 months** in one controlled setting. |
| Gain fades over time | **Open.** Point estimates fell about a quarter, but the intervals overlap heavily and control-arm adoption may explain part of it. The meta-analysis's "no decay" is unsupported because its evidence base was uncontrolled. |
| Mechanism | **Meetings are a substantial pathway** (registered test, about half of the gain, given the mediation assumptions). Fatigue is a smaller contributor, and about a third is unexplained. |
| Can reorganisation without cutting hours capture the gain? | **Open, and now the central policy question.** The evidence is two uncontrolled offices (+4.1%). Test: a three-arm trial comparing an hours cut, a meeting and workflow audit at full hours, and control. |
| Coverage-bound work | **Settled.** Output falls, and restoring service costs about 9% more per contact. The county ended the arm. |
| Timesheets understate hours | **Slightly, if logs measure total work.** The difference is about 1 point. |
| Generalising beyond one public employer, and to manufacturing | **Open.** |

Across the five documents, the conclusion that holds up is the following. In discretionary work, a 20% cut in scheduled hours yields roughly an 11–13% cut in actual hours and a durable gain of roughly 9–10% in output per actual hour. Output per worker is therefore close to maintained, sickness absence and resignations fall, and around half of the efficiency gain appears to come from removing low-value meeting time. In coverage-bound work, it costs output or money.

The open question is whether that meeting-driven half needs the hours cut at all, or whether the hours cut is what makes the reorganisation happen and last. Only a trial with a reorganisation-only arm can answer that.

I can draft the design for that three-arm trial, or write the combined evidence summary across all five documents.
